title: The Rapid Transformation of the Arctic
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Arctic is changing very fast. The region is warming three to four times faster than the rest of the world. Because of this, sea ice is melting quickly, the Greenland ice sheet is getting smaller, and frozen ground is starting to thaw out completely.
pages.caption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

imageProvenance.credit: Hunter Allen and Richard Rivera (NOAA’s Climate Program Office)http://www.climatewatch.noaa.gov/article/2011/arctic-warming-exceeds-global-average

evidence.articleCaption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

pages.text: These big changes affect animals and plants in nature. Tundra soil is getting warmer, so more plants and earthworms can grow there. Also, beavers are moving into northern rivers, and phytoplankton in the ocean are getting more sunlight and growing much more.
pages.caption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

evidence.articleCaption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

pages.text: Scientists think the Arctic Ocean will likely have its first ice-free summer days before the year 2050. This loss of sea ice makes life very hard for polar bears. Meanwhile, thawing permafrost is threatening buildings and valuable human infrastructure.
pages.caption: On average, climate change has lowered the thickness of land ice with every year, and reduced the extent of sea ice cover.

imageProvenance.credit: Thomas Slater, Isobel R. Lawrence, Inès N. Otosaka, Andrew Shepherd, Noel Gourmelen, Livia Jakob, Paul Tepes, Lin Gilbert, and Peter Nienow

evidence.articleCaption: On average, climate change has lowered the thickness of land ice with every year, and reduced the extent of sea ice cover.

pages.text: The loss of ice also causes problems far beyond the Arctic. Less ice means the whole planet absorbs more heat. Furthermore, melting ice sheets in Greenland add water to global seas, and thawing ground releases more carbon dioxide and methane gases.
pages.caption: Western Hemisphere Arctic Vegetation Index Trend

imageProvenance.credit: Ramakrishna Nemani of NASA’s Ames Research Center and Sangram Ganguly of the Bay Area Environmental Research Institute and NASA Ames

evidence.articleCaption: Western Hemisphere Arctic Vegetation Index Trend

pages.text: Sea ice in the region has been getting smaller and thinner for decades. It melts more in the summer than it grows back in winter. Because of global warming and greenhouse gases, this ice decline has grown much faster recently.

B1-B2.headline: The Rapid Transformation of the Arctic

pages.text: Climate change is transforming the Arctic at a speed among the highest on Earth, with temperatures rising three to four times faster than the global average. This rapid warming has driven a profound decline in Arctic sea ice, accelerated the melting of the Greenland ice sheet, and triggered widespread permafrost thaw that is expected to remain irreversible for centuries.
pages.caption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

imageProvenance.credit: Hunter Allen and Richard Rivera (NOAA’s Climate Program Office)http://www.climatewatch.noaa.gov/article/2011/arctic-warming-exceeds-global-average

evidence.articleCaption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

pages.text: Natural life across the region is responding strongly. Warmer tundra soils encourage the spread of boreal forests and make the land more hospitable to earthworms, while beavers colonize northern rivers. In the ocean, phytoplankton benefit from warmer waters and less shade, increasing marine primary production. However, ocean acidification threatens vulnerable zooplankton such as pteropods.
pages.caption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

evidence.articleCaption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

pages.text: The Arctic Ocean is expected to experience its first ice-free events before 2050, a situation with no precedent in the last 700,000 years. This shift threatens ice-dependent fauna like polar bears. At the same time, thawing permafrost endangers billions of dollars worth of northern infrastructure, and indigenous communities face the loss of their traditional way of life.
pages.caption: On average, climate change has lowered the thickness of land ice with every year, and reduced the extent of sea ice cover.

imageProvenance.credit: Thomas Slater, Isobel R. Lawrence, Inès N. Otosaka, Andrew Shepherd, Noel Gourmelen, Livia Jakob, Paul Tepes, Lin Gilbert, and Peter Nienow

evidence.articleCaption: On average, climate change has lowered the thickness of land ice with every year, and reduced the extent of sea ice cover.

pages.text: The consequences of these changes extend far beyond the polar region. Sea ice loss accelerates regional and global warming through the ice-albedo feedback loop, while permafrost thaw releases substantial greenhouse gases. Furthermore, the melting Greenland ice sheet contributes significantly to global sea level rise.
pages.caption: Western Hemisphere Arctic Vegetation Index Trend

imageProvenance.credit: Ramakrishna Nemani of NASA’s Ames Research Center and Sangram Ganguly of the Bay Area Environmental Research Institute and NASA Ames

evidence.articleCaption: Western Hemisphere Arctic Vegetation Index Trend

pages.text: Arctic sea ice has steadily declined in both area and volume over recent decades as summer melting outpaces winter refreezing. Driven by anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing, this decline has accelerated during the early twenty-first century, with summertime sea ice likely disappearing at some point during the twenty-first century.

C1-C2.headline: Climatic and Ecological Shifts in the Arctic

pages.text: Arctic climate change is driving transformations expected to be irreversible for centuries or millennia, with regional warming occurring at three to four times the global average. This unprecedented velocity has precipitated profound sea-ice decline, accelerated mass loss from the Greenland ice sheet, and initiated widespread permafrost degradation across the northern landscape.
pages.caption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

imageProvenance.credit: Hunter Allen and Richard Rivera (NOAA’s Climate Program Office)http://www.climatewatch.noaa.gov/article/2011/arctic-warming-exceeds-global-average

evidence.articleCaption: The image above shows where average air temperatures (October 2010 – September 2011) were up to 2 degrees Celsius above (red) or below (blue) the long-term average (1981–2010).

pages.text: Terrestrial and marine ecosystems are responding dynamically to these thermal shifts. Tundra soils are increasingly hospitable to boreal advancement and earthworm colonization, while beavers expand into northern watersheds, contributing to methane emissions. Concurrently, diminished ice cover has elevated marine primary production through enhanced phytoplankton proliferation, though concurrent ocean acidification severely threatens vulnerable calcifying zooplankton.
pages.caption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

evidence.articleCaption: The dark ocean surface reflects only 6 percent of incoming solar radiation, while sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent.

pages.text: Projections indicate the Arctic Ocean will likely experience ice-free conditions before 2050, an event without precedent in the last 700,000 years. This transition jeopardizes ice-dependent wildlife such as polar bears, while destabilizing billions of dollars of infrastructure anchored in thawing permafrost and challenging the heritage of indigenous populations.

pages.text: The ramifications of Arctic transformation transcend regional boundaries. Ice-albedo feedback exacerbates global thermal increases, and permafrost degradation releases greenhouse gas emissions comparable to major industrial nations. Additionally, sustained mass loss from Greenland constitutes a principal driver of global eustatic sea-level rise.

title: Understanding Yellow Fever
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Yellow fever is a viral disease. Most people have fever, chills, loss of appetite, nausea, and headaches. These symptoms usually get better within five days. In some cases, the illness comes back, causing liver damage and yellow skin.
pages.caption: Aedes aegypti feeding

evidence.articleCaption: Aedes aegypti feeding

pages.text: The disease is caused by a virus. It spreads through the bite of an infected mosquito. In cities, it spreads mainly through a type of mosquito called Aedes aegypti. This mosquito lives in tropical and subtropical parts of the world.
pages.caption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

imageProvenance.credit: Own scan, slightly modified. Original by Emil August Goeldi (1859 - 1917).

evidence.articleCaption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

pages.text: A safe and effective vaccine exists to prevent yellow fever. Many countries require travelers to get vaccinated. Other ways to prevent the disease include reducing mosquito populations and diagnosing cases early to stop outbreaks.
pages.caption: The cover of a certificate that confirms the holder has been vaccinated against yellow fever

evidence.articleCaption: The cover of a certificate that confirms the holder has been vaccinated against yellow fever

pages.text: Yellow fever is common in the tropical areas of South America and Africa, but it does not occur in Asia. Most cases happen in Africa. Since the 1980s, the number of cases has increased because more people live in cities and climates are changing.

pages.text: The disease originated in Africa. It spread to the Americas during the European trafficking of enslaved people. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, yellow fever caused major epidemics in many large cities around the world.

Yellow fever is a short viral illness with common early symptoms such as fever, chills, headaches, and muscle pains. While many people improve within five days, about fifteen percent experience a second phase. This severe stage brings abdominal pain, liver damage, and yellow skin.

C1-C2.headline: Epidemiology and Biology of Yellow Fever

pages.text: Yellow fever is an acute viral infection characterized initially by transient symptoms including pyrexia, myalgia, cephalalgia, and emesis. Although a majority of patients experience clinical improvement within five days, approximately fifteen percent progress to a more severe systemic phase marked by hepatocyte damage, jaundice, and elevated hemorrhagic risk.
pages.caption: Aedes aegypti feeding

evidence.articleCaption: Aedes aegypti feeding

pages.text: The causative agent is an RNA virus belonging to the genus Orthoflavivirus. Transmission occurs primarily via the vector Aedes aegypti in urban centers across tropical and subtropical zones. Due to clinical similarities with other pathologies, laboratory confirmation via polymerase chain reaction is necessary.
pages.caption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

imageProvenance.credit: Own scan, slightly modified. Original by Emil August Goeldi (1859 - 1917).

evidence.articleCaption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

pages.text: Immunization provides robust prophylaxis, leading many jurisdictions to mandate vaccination for incoming travelers. Vector reduction and early case identification remain critical control measures. Management for infected individuals is exclusively supportive, as specific antiviral interventions are ineffective.

pages.text: Endemic primarily in tropical regions of Africa and South America, the disease accounts for tens of thousands of severe infections annually. title: The Renaissance Dieppe Maps
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Dieppe maps are a group of large world maps and atlases. They were made in Dieppe, France, during the sixteenth century. Wealthy people and royal patrons, including kings, paid for these works.
pages.caption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Guillaume Brouscon. World chart, which includes America and a large Terra Java (Australia). HM 46. PORTOLAN ATLAS and NAUTICAL ALMANAC. France, 1543.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

pages.text: Many words on these maps are in French and Portuguese. Because of this, some people assumed the makers used old Portuguese sources. However, the maps are also known as great works of art.
pages.caption: Guillaume Le Testu's 1556 Cosmographie Universel, 4ème projection, where the northward extending promontory of the Terre australe is called Grande Jave.

evidence.articleCaption: Guillaume Le Testu's 1556 Cosmographie Universel, 4ème projection, where the northward extending promontory of the Terre australe is called Grande Jave.

pages.text: The maps show navigational lines and new discoveries, like Canada and Peru. They also show legends and mythical creatures, such as king Prester John and the Amazons in Russia.
pages.caption: World map of Nicolas Desliens, 1566.

evidence.articleCaption: World map of Nicolas Desliens, 1566.

pages.text: Most Dieppe maps show a big southern land called Jave la Grande. In modern times, many people in Australia have studied this feature to look for clues about early explorers.
pages.caption: Newspaper article of 4 February 1790

evidence.fileTitle: File:ORIGINAL DISCOVERY OF NEW HOLLAND, The Argus, 4 February 1790.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Newspaper article of 4 February 1790

pages.text: Experts say the maps mixed new geographical knowledge with very old ideas. They show how French mapmakers imagined the world during a time of big maritime trade and rivalry.

Produced in France during the 1540s, 1550s, and 1560s, the Dieppe maps are a series of large, hand-crafted world maps and atlases commissioned by wealthy patrons and royalty, including King Henry II of France and King Henry VIII of England.
pages.caption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Guillaume Brouscon. World chart, which includes America and a large Terra Java (Australia). HM 46. PORTOLAN ATLAS and NAUTICAL ALMANAC. France, 1543.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

pages.text: Because many inscriptions appear in French or Gallicised Portuguese, observers have often assumed that the Dieppe cartographers relied on secret Portuguese sources. The maps feature compass roses and rhumb lines, resembling sea charts, but they were primarily created as artistic display pieces meant to be spread out on tables.
pages.caption: Guillaume Le Testu's 1556 Cosmographie Universel, 4ème projection, where the northward extending promontory of the Terre australe is called Grande Jave.

evidence.articleCaption: Guillaume Le Testu's 1556 Cosmographie Universel, 4ème projection, where the northward extending promontory of the Terre australe is called Grande Jave.

pages.text: These works combined recent geographical discoveries—such as French attempts to colonize Canada, Spanish conquests in Peru, and Portuguese trade in the Spice Islands—with legendary elements like Cathay, Prester John, and Amazonian tribes. They also lacked any knowledge of longitude, which was common for maps made before the seventeenth century.
pages.caption: World map of Nicolas Desliens, 1566.

evidence.articleCaption: World map of Nicolas Desliens, 1566.

pages.text: A prominent feature on most Dieppe world maps is a large southern landmass known as Jave la Grande or Terra Australis. In the English-speaking world, public and academic interest over the past century and a half has focused heavily on whether this landmass indicates early Portuguese exploration of Australia.
pages.caption: Newspaper article of 4 February 1790

evidence.fileTitle: File:ORIGINAL DISCOVERY OF NEW HOLLAND, The Argus, 4 February 1790.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Newspaper article of 4 February 1790

pages.text: Recent scholarship suggests the maps reflect French territorial ambitions and geographic propaganda during a peak era of overseas trade. Rather than acting strictly as navigational records, they blended cutting-edge nautical information with medieval ideas and older global concepts derived from Ptolemy and Marco Polo.

The Dieppe school of cartography generated a substantial corpus of ornate world maps and atlases throughout the mid-sixteenth century. Commissioned by elite patrons, including monarchs like Henry II of France and Henry VIII of England, these hand-produced artifacts represented a pinnacle of contemporary European mapmaking.
pages.caption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

pages.text: Scholars have long debated the genesis of the Dieppe corpus. Linguistic analysis of French and Gallicised Portuguese inscriptions has frequently prompted the hypothesis that mapmakers utilized clandestine Portuguese cartographic intelligence, despite official state secrecy policies.

pages.text: While incorporating rhumb lines and navigational motifs characteristic of portolan charts, the maps functioned primarily as luxurious table atlases. They juxtaposed empirical data regarding contemporary territorial expansion with fantastical elements, medieval legends, and pre-modern geographical frameworks.

pages.text: A defining characteristic across the corpus is the depiction of the hypothetical southern continent, Terra Australis, incorporating the expansive promontory designated as Jave la Grande. Within modern Australian discourse, intense fascination has surrounded this specific feature as a potential indicator of early sixteenth-century Portuguese maritime contact.

pages.text: Historians emphasize that these cartographic works served as vehicles for geopolitical propaganda. They articulated French territorial aspirations and colonial rivalries while synthesizing disparate intellectual traditions, seamlessly merging cutting-edge navigational insights with enduring mythological conceptions of global space.

Produced in France during the 1540s, 1550s, and 1560s, the Dieppe maps are a series of large, hand-crafted world maps and atlases commissioned by wealthy patrons and royalty, including King Henry II of France and King Henry VIII of England.
pages.caption: A world map by Guillaume Brouscon, an example of a Dieppe map, 1543.

pages.text: Because many inscriptions appear in French or Gallicised Portuguese, observers have often assumed that the Dieppe cartographers relied on secret Portuguese sources. The maps feature compass roses and rhumb lines, resembling sea charts, but they were primarily created as artistic display pieces meant to be spread out on tables.
pages.caption: Guillaume Le Testu's 1556 Cosmographie Universel, 4ème projection, where the northward extending promontory of the Terre australe is called Grande Jave.

pages.text: These works combined recent geographical discoveries—such as French attempts to colonize Canada, Spanish conquests in Peru, and Portuguese trade in the Spice Islands—with legendary elements like Cathay, Prester John, and Amazonian tribes. They also lacked any knowledge of longitude, which was common for maps made before the seventeenth century.

pages.text: A prominent feature on most Dieppe world maps is a large southern landmass known as Jave la Grande or Terra Australis. In the English-speaking world, public and academic interest over the past century and a half has focused heavily on whether this landmass indicates early Portuguese exploration of Australia.

evidence.articleCaption: Newspaper article of 4 February 1790

pages.text: Recent scholarship suggests the maps reflect French territorial ambitions and geographic propaganda during a peak era of overseas trade. Rather than acting strictly as navigational records, they blended cutting-edge nautical information with medieval ideas and older global concepts derived from Ptolemy and Marco Polo.

pages.text: Anarchism is a political movement. It wants to end the state and capitalism. It tries to stop all rules and powers that hurt people. Anarchists want free groups to work together in peace.
pages.caption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Portrait Pierre-Joseph Proudhon by Nadar – BNF.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

pages.text: Long ago, ancient China and Greece had early ideas like this. Later, modern anarchism grew during the Enlightenment. The word comes from an old Greek term meaning without a leader.
pages.caption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

evidence.articleCaption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

pages.text: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first person to call himself an anarchist. He gave the word a good meaning. During the nineteenth century, different schools of anarchist thought began to form.
pages.caption: The Paris Commune, one of the earliest experiments of anarchism

evidence.articleCaption: The Paris Commune, one of the earliest experiments of anarchism

pages.text: Anarchists use many ways to change society. Some use slow and peaceful steps. Others want to destroy bad states quickly. They take part in workers' struggles and big historical revolutions.

pages.text: After World War II, the movement became small. But in the nineteen-sixties, anarchism grew again. Today, people in anti-war and anti-globalization groups help make the movement popular around the world.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Ideas of Anarchism

pages.text: Anarchism is a far-left political philosophy. It seeks to abolish institutions that perpetuate authority, coercion, or hierarchy, primarily targeting the state and capitalism. Anarchists advocate replacing these structures with stateless societies operating on free association and reciprocity.
pages.caption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Portrait Pierre-Joseph Proudhon by Nadar – BNF.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

pages.text: The term comes from the Ancient Greek word anarkhia, meaning without a ruler. While ancient precursors existed in China and Greece, modern anarchism emerged from the Enlightenment. Pierre-Joseph Proudhon later became the first political philosopher to proudly call himself an anarchist.
pages.caption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

evidence.articleCaption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

pages.text: During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the movement flourished worldwide. Anarchists participated in several major revolutions, including the Paris Commune and the Spanish Civil War. This classical era ended with the conclusion of the Spanish Civil War.
pages.caption: The Paris Commune, one of the earliest experiments of anarchism

evidence.articleCaption: The Paris Commune, one of the earliest experiments of anarchism

pages.text: Anarchists employ both evolutionary and revolutionary approaches to social change. Evolutionary methods favour gradual, often nonviolent reform, while revolutionary approaches seek to destroy oppressive states. Tactics have ranged from mass activism and strikes to militant resistance.
pages.caption: Mikhail Bakunin opposed the Marxist aim of dictatorship of the proletariat, aligning himself with the federalists in the First International before his expulsion by the Marxists.

evidence.articleCaption: Mikhail Bakunin opposed the Marxist aim of dictatorship of the proletariat, aligning himself with the federalists in the First International before his expulsion by the Marxists.

pages.text: By the end of World War II, the movement had weakened significantly. However, the 1960s witnessed a major revival tied to peace, environmental, and counterculture movements. In recent decades, anarchism has grown in influence within anti-capitalist and anti-globalisation campaigns.

Anarchism constitutes a predominantly far-left political current dedicated to dismantling hierarchical institutions that sustain coercion and authority, specifically focusing on the state and capitalist economics. Its adherents propose substituting these vertical systems with horizontal networks of voluntary associations grounded in reciprocity.
pages.caption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Portrait Pierre-Joseph Proudhon by Nadar – BNF.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist.

pages.text: Etymologically derived from the Greek anarkhia, denoting the absence of a ruler, the tradition found early philosophical precursors in Taoism and Stoicism. Although historical traces appear throughout history, modern anarchism crystallized during the Enlightenment, with Pierre-Joseph Proudhon pioneering the explicit self-identification.
pages.caption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

evidence.articleCaption: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), whose Republic inspired Peter Kropotkin

pages.text: The classical era spanned from the formation of distinct nineteenth-century schools until the Spanish Civil War. During this period, anarchists exerted substantial influence over labor movements and engaged in major historical uprisings, balancing theoretical diversity with militant direct action.
pages.caption: The Paris Commune, one of the earliest experiments of anarchism

pages.text: Strategic methodologies within the movement diverge into evolutionary and revolutionary categories. While evolutionary practitioners emphasize gradual, nonviolent transformation and counter-institutions, revolutionary factions historically and presently contemplate or execute direct confrontation against state apparatuses.

evidence.articleCaption: Mikhail Bakunin opposed the Marxist aim of dictatorship of the proletariat, aligning himself with the federalists in the First International before his expulsion by the Marxists.

pages.text: Following post-World War II contraction, the movement underwent a substantial resurgence during the 1960s amid disillusionment with Marxism-Leninism. Integrating with environmental, anti-nuclear, and New Left currents, contemporary anarchism continues to evolve through decentralized networks and anti-globalization activism.

pages.text: The Interoceanic Corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec is a trade and transit route in Southern Mexico. It connects the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans through a railway system. This project is under the control of the Mexican Secretariat of the Navy. It helps move both cargo and passengers across the isthmus.

pages.text: The project includes the modernization and expansion of local seaports. The main ports are Salina Cruz in Oaxaca and Coatzacoalcos in Veracruz. It also modernizes local oil refineries. The plan creates ten industrial parks in the isthmus area and two more parks in Chiapas to attract private investors.
